claims.text: Adding approximately 2–3 wt% copper to an HEA intermediate material will improve its heat-transfer capability.
Copper doping will form nanodispersed copper-rich precipitates at grain boundaries or within the HEA matrix.
The copper-rich precipitates will create localized electronic thermal-conduction pathways.
Localized copper-rich conduction pathways will increase electron-mediated heat transfer through the HEA.
Copper addition at approximately 2–3 wt% will not cause significant phase instability.
The dominant high-entropy-stabilized matrix will retain a robust microstructure after copper doping.
The copper-doped HEA will preserve mechanical strength, ductility, and phase stability.
The copper-doped HEA will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than the undoped HEA.
The proposed benefits will hold during cyclic exposure at approximately 600–800°C under high thermal flux and mechanical stress.
Temperatures of approximately 600–800°C, high thermal fluxes, and mechanical stresses are relevant operating conditions for plasma-facing reactor components.
Copper concentrations above approximately 2–3 wt% might produce detrimental segregation, microstructural changes, or loss of structural integrity.
Standard undoped HEA intermediate components are currently in use and have measured thermal and mechanical performance under comparable operating conditions.
The optimal dopant, concentration, and nanoscale formation mechanism are uncertain and require experimental verification.
